questions.title: Sections used for electron microscopic examination
questions.question: Which of the following is used for E.M examination?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Frozen sections preserve labile enzymes and fat for light-microscopic histochemistry, not electron microscopy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Paraffin sections are cut too thick and lack the resolution needed for the electron beam used in EM.
explanations.C: Correct. Plastic (resin) sections are cut ultrathin, on the order of 60 to 90 nanometres, which is thin enough for electrons to pass through them. Tissue destined for plastic embedding is fixed in glutaraldehyde and post-fixed in osmium tetroxide, which gives the strong contrast electron micrographs need. This combination of ultrathin sectioning and heavy-metal contrast is what makes plastic embedding the standard preparation for electron microscopy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hematoxylin and eosin is a light-microscopic stain applied to paraffin sections and has no role in electron microscopy.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: AUN-PMS-102 > Cytology > Microscopy and Specimen Preparation
questions.learning_objective: Identify plastic (resin) embedding as the specimen preparation required for electron microscopy.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Plastic sections" (Quiz 1 Q10).

questions.title: Principle of the electron microscope
questions.question: Which of the following is based on the passage of electron beams through the tissue?

explanations.A: Correct. The electron microscope forms its image by passing a beam of electrons through an ultrathin section and focusing the transmitted and scattered electrons with electromagnetic lenses onto a viewing screen or detector. Because electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light, this gives a resolving power thousands of times greater than the light microscope, which is why it can resolve organelle ultrastructure such as membranes and cristae. The specimen must therefore be cut ultrathin and heavy-metal stained, since a thick or unstained section would scatter or absorb the beam instead of transmitting it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cell culture is a technique for growing living cells outside the body and involves no electron beam at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acidic stains bind basic tissue components by chemical charge and are a light-microscopic histochemical method, not an imaging principle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The light microscope forms its image from visible light rays, not electron beams, which is exactly why its resolution is so much lower than the electron microscope's.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: AUN-PMS-102 > Cytology > Microscopy and Specimen Preparation
questions.learning_objective: Identify the electron microscope as the instrument that forms its image from a beam of electrons passing through the tissue.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Electron microscope" (Quiz 1 Q11).

questions.title: Bulk movement of macromolecules into the cell
questions.question: Bulk movement of macromolecules into the cell by formation of vesicles is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Exocytosis moves material out of the cell by fusing a cytoplasmic vesicle with the plasma membrane, the reverse direction of the process described.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A channel is an integral membrane protein that lets small molecules or ions cross the membrane directly, not a vesicle-forming process.
explanations.C: Correct. Endocytosis is the bulk movement of material into the cell by the plasma membrane forming a vesicle around it and pinching it off into the cytoplasm. It takes three forms: phagocytosis engulfs solid particles with pseudopodia, pinocytosis takes in extracellular fluid through small invaginations, and receptor-mediated endocytosis clusters ligand-bound receptors into a clathrin-coated pit that pinches off as a coated vesicle. All three share the same defining feature tested here, namely that material enters the cell packaged inside a membrane-bound vesicle rather than crossing the membrane directly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The fluid mosaic model describes the general structural organisation of the membrane's lipids and proteins, not a transport process.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify endocytosis as the vesicle-mediated bulk uptake of macromolecules into the cell.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Endocytosis" (Quiz 2 Q7).

questions.title: Peripheral membrane protein location
questions.question: ____ is bound to one of the two membrane surfaces, particularly on the cytoplasmic side.

explanations.A: Incorrect. An integral protein spans the whole bilayer rather than sitting loosely on a single surface, which is what distinguishes it from a peripheral protein.
explanations.B: Correct. A peripheral protein is loosely attached to only one face of the membrane, most often the cytoplasmic (inner) surface, and can be removed by mild treatments that do not disrupt the bilayer itself. Peripheral proteins commonly serve as enzymes or as part of the sub-membranous cytoskeleton that gives the membrane its mechanical support. Because they sit on a surface rather than crossing the bilayer, they are structurally and functionally distinct from the transmembrane integral proteins.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Carbohydrate is attached only to the external (outer) face of the membrane as glycolipid or glycoprotein, not to the cytoplasmic side.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lipid bilayer is the membrane's structural framework itself, not a protein bound to one of its surfaces.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Locate peripheral membrane proteins to one membrane surface, most often the cytoplasmic face, in contrast to transmembrane integral proteins.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Peripheral protein" (Quiz 2 Q8).

questions.title: The bilayer-forming lipid of the plasma membrane
questions.question: In plasma membrane, ____ are organized into a double layer (bilayer):

explanations.A: Incorrect. Peripheral protein sits on one membrane surface and does not itself form the bilayer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cholesterol molecules are interspersed among the phospholipid tails to stabilise the membrane, but it is the phospholipid, not cholesterol, that forms the bilayer's basic architecture.
explanations.C: Correct. The plasma membrane's lipid is phospholipid, arranged as a bilayer with the hydrophilic (water-loving) heads facing the aqueous solutions on either side and the hydrophobic (water-fearing) fatty-acid tails directed inward toward each other. This amphipathic arrangement is what lets the membrane act as a barrier between the cytoplasm and the extracellular fluid while still allowing embedded proteins to float within it. Cholesterol, integral and peripheral proteins, and carbohydrate are all additional components carried within or upon this phospholipid bilayer rather than components that themselves form it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Carbohydrate is attached to lipid and protein on the membrane's outer face only and does not form the bilayer.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify phospholipid as the bilayer-forming lipid of the plasma membrane.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Phospholipids." (Quiz 2 Q9).

questions.title: Protein embedded within the phospholipid bilayer
questions.question: What is directly incorporated within the phospholipid bilayer?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The sugar chain of a glycolipid projects from the outer surface of the bilayer; it is not itself embedded within it.
explanations.B: Correct. Integral (transmembrane) proteins are directly incorporated within the phospholipid bilayer, spanning it from the cytoplasmic to the extracellular face. Because they cross the bilayer, they are positioned to act as channel proteins that let ions and water pass and as carrier proteins for small polar molecules such as glucose, unlike a peripheral protein that only rests on one surface. Removing an integral protein generally requires disrupting the bilayer itself, which is the practical test that distinguishes it from a loosely attached peripheral protein.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A peripheral protein rests loosely on one membrane surface rather than being incorporated within the bilayer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The sugar chain of a glycoprotein also projects from the external surface and is not embedded within the bilayer.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The cell coat (glycocalyx) is the carbohydrate-rich layer coating the outer surface of the membrane, not a structure embedded within the bilayer itself.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify the integral (transmembrane) protein as the component directly embedded within the phospholipid bilayer.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Integral protein" (Quiz 2 Q10).

questions.title: The powerhouse of the cell
questions.question: The power house of the cell is:

explanations.A: Correct. Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell, sited in its most metabolically active regions and bounded by two unit membranes. The outer membrane is smooth and permeable to small molecules, while the inner membrane folds inward into cristae bearing the elementary particles that carry ATP synthase activity. The matrix inside holds the citric-acid-cycle enzymes and mitochondrial DNA, and it is this whole arrangement of membranes and matrix enzymes that lets mitochondria generate the cell's ATP.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Golgi bodies pack, modify and route secretory proteins; they do not generate the cell's ATP supply.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum synthesises lipids and detoxifies substances, a function unrelated to ATP generation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rough endoplasmic reticulum synthesises and processes proteins destined for secretion or membranes, not ATP.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify the mitochondrion as the organelle that generates the cell's ATP.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Mitochondria" (Quiz 6&7 Q9).

questions.title: Organelle composed of stacked cisternae and vesicles
questions.question: ____ is composed of several array of cisternae and vesicles:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A ribosome is a small ribonucleoprotein particle, not an array of membranous cisternae.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is built of interconnected tubules and vesicles rather than the stacked flat cisternae characteristic of the Golgi.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mitochondria are bounded by two unit membranes folded into cristae, a different architecture from stacked cisternae.
explanations.D: Correct. On electron microscopy the Golgi apparatus is a stack of three to ten interconnected, parallel, flat curved saccules (cisternae) lying one above another, with vesicles clustered at both ends of the stack. The entry (cis) face receives transfer vesicles from the rough endoplasmic reticulum, and the exit (trans) face buds off the secretory vesicles, lysosomes and coated vesicles that the Golgi produces. This stack-of-cisternae-with-vesicles architecture is exactly what the question describes and is unique among the organelles listed.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify the Golgi apparatus as the stack of cisternae and vesicles seen on electron microscopy.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Golgi bodies" (Quiz 6&7 Q10).

questions.title: Function of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum
questions.question: Smooth ER:

options.A: Is the digestive apparatus of cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lysosome, not smooth ER, is the digestive apparatus of the cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Protein synthesis is carried out by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum, which is exactly what its studded, ribosome-covered surface is for; smooth ER has no attached ribosomes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Packing and chemically modifying secretory material is the Golgi apparatus's job, performed as the material passes from its entry to its exit face.
explanations.D: Correct. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum, a system of ribosome-free tubules continuous with the rough ER, is the site of lipid and steroid synthesis and of the enzymatic detoxification of drugs and other harmful substances, work that is especially prominent in liver cells. Because it carries no ribosomes it is identified in electron micrographs as an acidophilic, tubular network distinct from the ribosome-studded rough ER. These two functions, lipid synthesis and detoxification, are the defining roles tested here.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that smooth endoplasmic reticulum synthesises lipids and detoxifies substances.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Makes lipids, and inactivates toxins" (Quiz 6&7 Q11); duplicate-of Quiz 6&7 Q19 (p18, "organelle involved in lipid metabolism" -> SER), not authored twice.

questions.title: Rod-shaped organelle with many inner folds
questions.question: Which of the following cell organelles is rod shaped with many inner folds?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rough endoplasmic reticulum is a flattened system of ribosome-studded membranes, not a rod-shaped, folded organelle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Golgi bodies form a stack of flat curved cisternae, not a rod-shaped structure with inner folds.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is a tubular network, not a rod-shaped organelle.
explanations.D: Correct. Mitochondria are typically rod-shaped or granular organelles bounded by two unit membranes, of which the inner membrane folds repeatedly inward to form cristae that project into the central matrix. This folding greatly increases the surface area available for the elementary particles carrying ATP synthase activity, which is why the organelle's inner-membrane folding is functionally as well as structurally distinctive. Iron haematoxylin and Janus green stains are used to identify mitochondria under the light microscope by exactly this rod or granular shape.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Recognise the mitochondrion's rod shape and inner-membrane folding (cristae) as its defining structural features.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Mitochondria." (Quiz 6&7 Q12).

questions.title: Function of the Golgi body
questions.question: Golgi Body:

explanations.A: Correct. The Golgi apparatus packs, concentrates and chemically modifies protein as it moves from its cis (entry) face to its trans (exit) face, most notably by adding carbohydrate to convert protein into glycoprotein. From the trans face it also buds off secretory vesicles, primary lysosomes and coated vesicles, and it renews the plasma membrane by sending membrane to it. Modifying and packaging protein this way, not synthesising it in the first place, is the Golgi's defining role.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Protein synthesis is carried out by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum, which then hands its product to the Golgi for modification, not the other way round.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Digestion and recycling of material is the job of the lysosome, which the Golgi only helps to package.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ATP production is the mitochondrion's role, not the Golgi apparatus's.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the Golgi apparatus packages and chemically modifies protein, most notably by glycosylation.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Modifies proteins" (Quiz 6&7 Q13).

questions.title: Organelle bounded by a smooth outer and folded inner membrane
questions.question: ____ are surrounded by two membranes; the outer is smooth and the inner is folded:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ribosomes are small ribonucleoprotein particles with no membrane at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Golgi bodies are a single stack of flat cisternae, not an organelle bounded by two membranes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lysosomes are bounded by a single membrane, not by an outer and an inner one.
explanations.D: Correct. Mitochondria are bounded by two unit membranes: a smooth outer membrane that carries porins and is freely permeable to small molecules, and a selectively permeable inner membrane that folds inward into cristae. This two-membrane, smooth-outer/folded-inner arrangement is what physically separates the intermembrane space from the matrix and is the organelle's most recognisable ultrastructural feature.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Describe the mitochondrion's two-membrane envelope: a smooth outer membrane and a folded (cristae-forming) inner membrane.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: MMitochondria" (Quiz 6&7 Q14).

questions.title: Origin of secretory granules
questions.question: Secretory granules:

options.B: Originate as condensing vesicles from the Golgi bodies
options.D: Are released from cells by phagocytosis

explanations.A: Incorrect. A catalase-containing granule describes a peroxisome, not a secretory granule.
explanations.B: Correct. Secretory granules originate as condensing vesicles budded from the trans (exit) face of the Golgi apparatus, where secretory protein is concentrated and packaged after being modified there. As a condensing vesicle matures into a mature secretory granule its contents become progressively denser, ready for eventual release from the cell by exocytosis. This Golgi origin is what distinguishes a secretory granule from a lysosome or a peroxisome, which arise by different pathways.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A secretory granule is bounded by a single membrane, not two, which is what lets it fuse with and merge into the single-membraned plasma membrane during exocytosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Secretory granules release their contents by exocytosis, the fusion of the granule membrane with the plasma membrane, not by phagocytosis, which is a form of uptake into the cell.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that secretory granules originate as condensing vesicles budded from the Golgi's trans face.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Originate as condensing vesicles from the Golgi bodies" (Quiz 6&7 Q15).

questions.title: Microbodies (peroxisomes) contain catalase
questions.question: Microbodies:

options.C: Are secondary lysosomes containing indigestible materials

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acid phosphatase activity is a marker enzyme of the lysosome, not the microbody.
explanations.B: Correct. Microbodies (peroxisomes) hold oxidase enzymes that generate hydrogen peroxide as a by-product of their oxidative reactions, together with the enzyme catalase, which then breaks that hydrogen peroxide down before it can damage the cell. This oxidase-plus-catalase pairing is the defining biochemical feature of the peroxisome. Peroxisomes are especially abundant in liver and kidney cells, which do a large share of the body's oxidative detoxification work.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A residual body is the secondary lysosome that contains indigestible material, a different organelle from the microbody.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Microbodies are most abundant in liver and kidney cells, not muscle cells.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that microbodies (peroxisomes) hold oxidases and the catalase that destroys their hydrogen peroxide by-product.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Contain catalase" (Quiz 6&7 Q16).

questions.title: Cristae of the mitochondrion
questions.question: Cristae are:

options.A: The membranous infoldings of the outer membrane of mitochondria
options.B: The membranous infoldings of the inner membrane of mitochondria
options.C: The jelly like central matrix of mitochondria
options.D: Enzymes located on the outer mitochondrial membrane

explanations.A: Incorrect. The outer mitochondrial membrane is smooth and does not fold into cristae; folding is confined to the inner membrane.
explanations.B: Correct. Cristae are the membranous infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane, projecting into the central matrix and greatly increasing the membrane's surface area. Studding the cristae are elementary particles that carry ATP synthase activity, which is what makes the folding functionally worthwhile rather than merely a structural curiosity. Describing cristae as folds without naming this ATP-synthase role misses the reason the inner membrane is folded in the first place.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The jelly-like central compartment of the mitochondrion is the matrix, a separate structure from the membranous cristae.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cristae are membranous infoldings, not enzymes, and they belong to the inner membrane, not the outer one.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Define cristae as the inner-membrane infoldings of the mitochondrion that carry the ATP synthase elementary particles.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: The membranous infolding's of the inner membrane of mitochondria" (Quiz 6&7 Q17).

questions.title: Stain used to visualize mitochondria
questions.question: Which of the following stains is used to visualize mitochondria?

explanations.A: Correct. Mitochondria are identified under the light microscope as rods or granules stained by iron haematoxylin or, classically, by Janus green, a supravital dye that mitochondria reduce and retain because of their active oxidative enzymes. Janus green stains living mitochondria a distinctive blue-green while other cell structures remain largely unstained, which is exactly what makes it a specific and reliable marker for this organelle. This selectivity is why it remains the classic light-microscopic stain for demonstrating mitochondria.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acid phosphatase is an enzyme histochemical marker for lysosomes, not a mitochondrial stain.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A silver impregnation method is used to demonstrate reticular fibres or the Golgi apparatus, not mitochondria specifically.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Plain haematoxylin is a general basophilic nuclear stain; it is iron haematoxylin specifically, not ordinary haematoxylin, that is used to demonstrate mitochondria.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that Janus green is the classic supravital stain used to visualise mitochondria.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Janus green" (Quiz 6&7 Q18).

questions.title: Secretory transport pathway through the ER, Golgi and lysosome
questions.question: The endoplasmic reticulum acts as a transporting system. Choose the correct path of transport of substances:

explanations.A: Incorrect. This reverses the true sequence: material does not travel back out of the lysosome into the rough ER.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This also puts the pathway in reverse order, starting from the Golgi rather than ending there.
explanations.C: Correct. Newly synthesised protein begins on ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum, which packages it into transfer vesicles that travel to the Golgi apparatus's entry (cis) face. The Golgi concentrates, chemically modifies and sorts the protein as it moves toward the trans (exit) face, from which it buds off as a primary lysosome or another vesicle type. This rough-ER-to-Golgi-to-lysosome sequence is the classic secretory/lysosomal transport pathway that links protein synthesis to its final packaged destination.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This route starts from the lysosome, the pathway's end point, rather than from the rough ER where protein synthesis begins.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Sequence the secretory transport pathway from the rough ER through the Golgi to the lysosome.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Rough ER - Golgi - Lysosome" (Quiz 6&7 Q20).

questions.title: The coronal plane
questions.question: The plane which divides the body into anterior and posterior parts is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A transverse plane divides the body into upper and lower parts, not anterior and posterior.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mid-sagittal plane divides the body into right and left halves along the midline.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A sagittal plane, like the mid-sagittal plane, divides the body into right and left parts, not front and back.
explanations.D: Correct. A coronal (frontal) plane is a vertical plane running at a right angle to the sagittal plane, dividing the body into an anterior (front) part and a posterior (back) part. It is one of the three fundamental anatomical planes used to describe body sections, alongside the sagittal plane (right/left) and the transverse plane (upper/lower). Distinguishing the coronal plane by the specific anterior/posterior division it produces is essential for describing radiographic and cross-sectional anatomy correctly.

questions.subject: msk
questions.module_subject: AUN-PMS-102 > General Anatomy > Anatomical Terms and Planes
questions.learning_objective: Identify the coronal (frontal) plane as the plane dividing the body into anterior and posterior parts.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Coronal" (Quiz 9 Q1).

questions.title: The transverse plane
questions.question: The ____ plane divides the body into upper and lower parts:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The coronal plane divides the body into anterior and posterior parts, not upper and lower.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mid-sagittal plane divides the body into right and left halves.
explanations.C: Correct. A transverse (horizontal, axial) plane runs at a right angle to the body's long axis, dividing it into an upper (superior) part and a lower (inferior) part. It is the third of the three fundamental anatomical planes, alongside the sagittal (right/left) and coronal (anterior/posterior) planes, and is the plane most familiar from cross-sectional imaging such as CT. Recognising which of the three planes produces an upper/lower division is what this question is testing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A sagittal plane divides the body into right and left parts, not upper and lower.

questions.subject: msk
questions.module_subject: AUN-PMS-102 > General Anatomy > Anatomical Terms and Planes
questions.learning_objective: Identify the transverse plane as the plane dividing the body into upper and lower parts.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Transverse" (Quiz 9 Q2).

questions.title: The anatomical term "medial"
questions.question: ____ is a structure situated nearer to the median plane of the body than another is said to be.

explanations.A: Correct. In standard anatomical terminology, a structure is described as medial when it lies nearer to the body's median (mid-sagittal) plane than a structure it is being compared with. This term is one of a paired set used to describe the relative position of one structure against another along the side-to-side axis. Its counterpart, lateral, describes the opposite relationship, a structure lying farther from the median plane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lateral describes a structure farther from the median plane, the opposite of what the stem describes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Superior describes a structure nearer the head along the vertical axis, an unrelated comparison to nearness to the median plane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Distal describes a structure farther from the trunk or point of origin of a limb, a comparison along the proximal-distal axis rather than nearness to the median plane.

questions.subject: msk
questions.module_subject: AUN-PMS-102 > General Anatomy > Anatomical Terms and Planes
questions.learning_objective: Define medial as nearer to the median plane, distinguishing it from lateral, superior and distal.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: medial" (Quiz 9 Q3).

questions.title: The patella as the knee cap
questions.question: Which of the following is known as knee cap?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The clavicle is the collar bone of the shoulder girdle, unrelated to the knee.
explanations.B: Correct. The patella, commonly called the knee cap, is a sesamoid bone, meaning it develops within the tendon of the quadriceps femoris muscle rather than forming a joint directly between two long bones. It lies anterior to the knee joint and glides within the femoral trochlear groove as the knee flexes and extends, protecting the joint and improving the mechanical leverage of the quadriceps tendon. Being the largest sesamoid bone in the body is what makes the patella the classic example taught for this bone category.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The acetabulum is the cup-shaped socket of the hip bone that receives the head of the femur, not the knee cap.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The scapula is the shoulder blade, a flat bone of the shoulder girdle unrelated to the knee.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: Identify the patella as the sesamoid bone commonly known as the knee cap.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Patella" (Quiz 9 Q4).

questions.title: The humerus as a long bone
questions.question: The humerus is ____ bone.

explanations.A: Correct. Anatomical bone classification by shape recognises four categories: long, short, flat and irregular bones. The humerus, the single bone of the arm running from the shoulder to the elbow, is a long bone, meaning it has a shaft (diaphysis) that is greater in length than in width and two expanded ends (epiphyses). This shaft-and-two-ends structure is the defining feature that places any given bone in the long-bone category, and it is what places the humerus there.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An irregular bone, such as a vertebra, has a complex shape that fits none of the other three categories, unlike the humerus's simple shaft-and-ends structure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A short bone is roughly as wide as it is long, such as a carpal bone, unlike the elongated humerus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A flat bone is thin and plate-like, such as the sternum or a skull bone, a shape that does not describe the humerus.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: Classify the humerus as a long bone within the long/short/flat/irregular bone-shape system.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: long" (Quiz 9 Q5).

questions.title: The vertebra as an irregular bone
questions.question: The vertebra is ____ bone.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A short bone, such as a carpal bone, is roughly cuboidal in shape, a description that does not fit the vertebra's complex form.
explanations.B: Correct. A vertebra is classified as an irregular bone because its shape, a body plus a vertebral arch bearing several processes, does not fit the simple long, short or flat categories. Irregular bones are grouped together precisely because their complex, individually distinctive shapes serve specialised local functions rather than the generic support or protection roles of the other categories. The vertebra is the standard teaching example of an irregular bone for exactly this reason.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A flat bone, such as the sternum, is thin and plate-like, unlike the vertebra's complex shape.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A long bone has a shaft longer than it is wide with two expanded ends, a description that does not fit the vertebra.

questions.title: Circumduction as a combination of movements
questions.question: Circumduction is a circular movement that is a combination of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Supination and pronation are rotational movements of the forearm, a pair distinct from the four movements that combine to produce circumduction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Medial and lateral rotation are separate rotational movements about the long axis of a bone, not the movements that combine into circumduction.
explanations.C: Correct. Circumduction is a circular, cone-shaped movement produced by combining flexion, extension, abduction and adduction in sequence around a joint, without any independent rotation of its own. It is possible at joints with enough range of movement to perform all four of these component movements, such as the shoulder and hip. Because it is built entirely from those four already-described movements rather than being a fifth, separate movement type, it is correctly taught as their combination.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inversion and eversion are movements specific to the foot at the subtalar joint, unrelated to circumduction.

questions.title: Smooth muscle in visceral organs
questions.question: ____ makes up the muscular portion of the various visceral organs.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Not all three muscle types line visceral organs, so "all of the above" is wrong; only smooth muscle does.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cardiac muscle is confined to the myocardium of the heart, not the walls of the other visceral organs.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Skeletal muscle is attached to the skeleton and moves the body voluntarily; it does not form the wall of visceral organs.
explanations.D: Correct. Of the three muscle types, told apart by where they are, whether they are voluntary, whether they are striated, and which nerves supply them, smooth muscle is the one found in the walls of blood vessels and viscera such as the gut, bladder and uterus. It contracts involuntarily under autonomic nerve supply and shows no cross-striations under the microscope, unlike skeletal or cardiac muscle. This visceral location, together with its involuntary, unstriated character, is what makes smooth muscle the muscular component of hollow visceral organs.

questions.title: Bipennate muscle fibre arrangement
questions.question: ____ have two rows of muscle fibers, with a central tendon, like a feather.

explanations.A: Correct. Skeletal muscles are classified by the arrangement of their fibres, and pennate muscles have fibres set obliquely on a tendon like the barbs of a feather. A bipennate muscle, such as rectus femoris, has its tendon running down the middle with two rows of fibres attaching obliquely on both sides of it, exactly the feather-like arrangement described. This packs more, shorter fibres into the same volume than a parallel arrangement would, giving a pennate muscle more power at the cost of a smaller range of movement.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A fusiform muscle is spindle-shaped with fibres running the length of the muscle, not arranged in two feather-like rows around a central tendon.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A parallel (strap-like) muscle, such as sartorius, has fibres running the muscle's whole length, unlike the oblique, feather-like arrangement of bipennate muscle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A unipennate muscle, such as flexor pollicis longus, has its tendon running along only one side with a single row of oblique fibres, not two rows on either side of a central tendon.
